title: How do you multiply big numbers in your head without losing the zeros?
description: Big numbers without losing the zeros: a quick way to do this case calculation in your head, with a worked example.
hook: Split every number into a small number and a count of zeros, multiply the small numbers, then add the zeros back at the end. Big numbers trip people up because of the zeros, not the maths, and this one habit keeps them under control when you are working out loud.
body:
The method

4.5 million customers each pay $300 a year. What is the revenue?
  1. Split each number into a small part and its zeros: 4.5M = 4.5 × 10⁶ and 300 = 3 × 10².
  2. Multiply the small parts: 4.5 × 3 = 13.5.
  3. Add the zeros: 10⁶ × 10² = 10⁸.
  4. Combine: 13.5 × 10⁸ = 1,350,000,000, or $1.35B.

The arithmetic you actually do is 4.5 × 3. Everything else is bookkeeping, and bookkeeping is easy if you keep it separate.

How to say it in the interview

"Revenue is customers times spend per customer. That's 4.5 million times $300. Four and a half times three is 13.5, and I have six zeros from the million plus two from the 300, so eight in total: $1.35 billion a year."

Saying the zero count out loud lets the interviewer follow and catch a slip before it spreads into the rest of the case. Then add the so-what: "That's about three times the client's current revenue, so even a small share of this market would matter."

Division works the same way

Cancel zeros before you divide. A market worth $2.4B has 80,000 business customers. What does each spend?

  • $2.4B = 2.4 × 10⁹, and 80,000 = 8 × 10⁴.
  • 2.4 ÷ 8 = 0.3.
  • 10⁹ ÷ 10⁴ = 10⁵.
  • 0.3 × 10⁵ = $30,000 per customer.

If you prefer to avoid powers of ten, strike the same number of zeros from top and bottom: 2,400,000,000 ÷ 80,000 becomes 240,000 ÷ 8 = 30,000.

Keep the scale visible until the end

A second route through the first example is to work in millions: 4.5 million × 3 × 100 = 13.5 million × 100 = 1,350 million, which is $1.35B. If two routes agree, you can be confident.

Then sanity-check against an anchor you know: 1 million people paying $1,000 a year is $1B. The example has 4.5 times as many people paying 30% as much, so 4.5 × 0.3 = 1.35, or $1.35B. It matches.

Keep these conversions to hand:

WordZerosWritten
Thousand (k)3$450k = $450,000
Million (M)6$2.4M = $2,400,000
Billion (B)9$1.35B = $1,350M

Common mistakes

  • Mixing millions and billions mid-answer. Write the unit next to every intermediate number and convert only at the end.
  • Losing a zero in "hundreds of thousands". 350k × 1,200 is 3.5 × 1.2 = 4.2, with 5 + 3 = 8 zeros: 420M. It is easy to say 42M by mistake.
  • Forgetting time units. A monthly figure needs × 12 before it becomes yearly revenue. 60M people paying $25 a month is $18B a year, not $1.5B.
  • Skipping the check. If revenue per customer comes out at $3 for a car, or $30,000 for a coffee, you have lost three zeros somewhere.

Practice

1. 28M UK households each spend $120 a year on a product. What is the market worth?

Show the answer

2.8 × 1.2 = 3.36. Zeros: seven from 28M (it is 2.8 × 10⁷) and two from 120 (1.2 × 10²), so nine. Answer: $3.36B a year.

2. Revenue is $7.2B and there are 900,000 customers. What is revenue per customer?

Show the answer

7.2 ÷ 9 = 0.8. Zeros: 10⁹ ÷ 10⁵ = 10⁴. So 0.8 × 10⁴ = $8,000 per customer. Check: 900,000 × $8,000 = 7.2 × 10⁹.

3. A chain sells 350,000 units at $1,200 each. What is revenue?

Show the answer

3.5 × 1.2 = 4.2. Zeros: five from 350,000 and three from 1,200, so eight. Answer: $420M.

Where to practise next

Big numbers matter most in market sizing, so try them in a full estimate such as sizing the US dog food market or the market sizing drill. For speed, use the case maths drill, and for the rest of the shortcuts see the case maths cheat sheet.
